newsitem.title: USA: FCC near accord on plan to cut long-distance rates.
newsitem.headline: FCC near accord on plan to cut long-distance rates.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission is near agreement on a plan designed to deliver consumers the largest cut in long-distance phone rates ever, the chairman of the agency said Saturday.

The plan would reduce by $1.7 billion the fees long-distance carriers pay local phone companies to access their networks. In a significant development, AT&T Corp has promised to pass on all of the savings to all its customers with rate cuts of 5 percent to 15 percent.
"That is the key that unlocks the door," FCC Chairman Reed Hundt said in an interview.

Agency officials have been racing to negotiate an overhaul of the nation's charges and subsidies that are designed to keep phone service affordable for all Americans. The revamp stems from last year's big telecommunications law.

While crafting the overhaul, FCC officials also must find an additional $2 billion to $3 billion a year to hook up schools, libraries and hospitals to the Internet computer network. The agency is scheduled to vote on the plan next week.

Agency officials said the latest breakthrough came after AT&T agreed to pass along to consumers all the savings it receives from at least a $1.7 billion cut in the $23 billion annually long distance companies pay local carriers to access their networks.
FCC officials previously had been considering a $1 billion reduction -- a figure long-distance companies deemed too low.

If given at least a $1.7 billion access-charge cut, AT&T promised the FCC to reduce its daytime and evening rates by 5 percent and to reduce its nighttime and weekend rates by 15 percent. The cut would go to all customers -- including residential customers who are not on a special calling plan.

These basic-rate customers have faced rate hikes in the past three to five years. By contrast, previous access-rate reductions have been passed on to the carrier's business customers and residential customers who are on a special calling plan.

FCC officials estimate the $1.7 billion reduction would amount to a rate cut of a little more than $600 million for AT&T customers. Other long-distance carriers would then be under pressure to match the reductions.
Hundt said he believes that at least three of the FCC's four commissioners can agree to the plan. "I'm quite, quite hopeful," he said.

Hundt said the agency must still work out other details of its overhaul of access charges and affordable, or "universal," phone-service rules. A key sticking point has been a proposal by Hundt that would require businesses with more than one phone -- but which make few long-distance calls -- to pay more for their additional lines.
